opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is that a lot of the value inside a company sits in data that no general-purpose model has ever seen. The big models are trained on public web data, which makes them very good generalists, but they don't know your internal processes, your codebase, your customer interactions, your domain vocabulary. When you take a strong base model and train it further on your own data, you get something that understands your specific problems much better, and often a much smaller model can match or beat a much larger general model on those tasks. That matters a lot for cost and latency once you're running at scale.

There's also a control aspect. If your whole product depends on a model behind someone else's API, you don't control when it changes, how it's priced, or where your data goes. Many companies, especially in regulated industries like banking, healthcare, or defense, simply can't send sensitive data outside. Being able to train and deploy on your own infrastructure, with weights you actually own, solves that.

And finally, I think it's a question of differentiation. If everyone uses the same off-the-shelf model with the same prompts, nobody has an edge. Your proprietary data is your moat, and fine-tuning or continued pretraining is how you turn that data into a model that's actually yours. That's a big part of why we've cared so much about releasing strong open-weight models and giving customers the tools to customize them, rather than just offering a single black box.

r001.rationale: It says company data contains internal processes, code, customer interactions, and domain vocabulary that public-web-trained models do not know.

r002.rationale: It says training on company data improves task performance, but does not compare that with supplying the data as inference-time context.

r003.rationale: It says a smaller model can beat a larger general model, but does not claim it can outperform a closed-source alternative.

r004.rationale: It does not say training reduces the need to repeat company knowledge in each query's context.

r005.rationale: It says proprietary data can create a moat and that using the same off-the-shelf model as competitors leaves companies without an edge.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the main reason is that the data a company has is, in most cases, the only real differentiator it has. The base models are becoming more and more similar. If you take any of the strong open-weight models today, the capabilities are quite close, and in a year they will be even closer. So the question becomes: what makes your model better for your use case than the model your competitor can download tomorrow? And the answer is almost always the data.

When we were at Meta, and then when we started Mistral, we saw this over and over. A model that is fine-tuned on a few thousand or a few tens of thousands of examples from a specific domain, with the specific format, the specific vocabulary, the specific edge cases that customers actually hit, will very often beat a much larger general model on that task. Not on MMLU, but on the thing you actually care about. And that gap does not go away just because the general model gets bigger, because the general model has never seen your internal documents, your tickets, your logs, your code base.

There is also a second reason, which is more practical. If you train on your own data, you control the model. You can run it on-premise, you know exactly what went into it, you can update it when your data changes, and you are not dependent on an API whose behavior changes under you every few months. For a lot of enterprises, especially in Europe, in finance, in healthcare, this is not a nice-to-have. They simply cannot send their data to a third party.

And honestly, it is much easier than people think. Two years ago, fine-tuning meant a team of researchers and a lot of GPUs. Today the open models are good enough that a small team can take a 7B or a 20B model, fine-tune it in a day, and get something very competitive. The barrier is not the compute anymore, it is mostly having the data cleaned and in the right format. So my advice is usually: start small, pick one task where you have good data, and see how far you get. Most people are surprised.

r001.rationale: It says general models have never seen a company’s internal documents, tickets, logs, or code base, identifying company-specific knowledge unavailable to those models.

r002.rationale: It says fine-tuning can improve performance on a specific task, but does not compare training with supplying company data as inference-time context.

r003.rationale: It says fine-tuning can beat a larger general model, but does not claim it can outperform a closed-source alternative.

r004.rationale: It does not say training reduces the need to provide company knowledge repeatedly with each query.

r005.rationale: It explicitly asks what makes a model better for a company’s use case than a model its competitor can download and answers: “almost always, the data.”

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that a lot of the knowledge that matters to a company is private. It’s in internal documents, code, or interactions with customers, so a model trained on public data won’t have access to it. Training on that data can help a model learn the company’s terminology and adapt to the tasks people actually need it to do.

That doesn’t necessarily mean training a model from scratch. You can start with a pretrained model and fine-tune it. And sometimes retrieval is enough—if you just need to look up information, you may not need additional training. The question is whether you want to give the model access to facts or teach it to perform a particular task better.

r001.rationale: It says important company knowledge is private and unavailable to a model trained only on public data.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes training to improve task performance from retrieval for facts, but does not claim training incorporates knowledge more effectively than supplying it at inference.

r003.rationale: It mentions fine-tuning a pretrained model but makes no comparison with closed-source alternatives.

r004.rationale: It does not say that training avoids repeatedly supplying company knowledge in query context.

r005.rationale: It does not claim company data can differentiate a model from competitors’ models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the value comes from data that isn’t available on the internet. A company has internal documents, code, and knowledge about its business that a general-purpose model has never seen. Training on that data can make a model much more useful for the specific problems the company wants to solve.

And you don’t necessarily need to train a huge model from scratch. You can start with a pretrained model and adapt it. If your task is fairly narrow, a smaller, specialized model can be very effective, while also being cheaper to run and easier to deploy within your own infrastructure.

r001.rationale: It says company internal documents, code, and business knowledge are not available on the internet and unseen by general-purpose models.

r002.rationale: It does not compare training on company data with supplying that data as inference-time context.

r003.rationale: It does not claim that fine-tuning can outperform a closed-source alternative.

r004.rationale: It does not say that training avoids repeatedly providing company knowledge with each query.

r005.rationale: It does not describe proprietary-data training as a way to distinguish a model from competitors’ models.
